Key findings from the permissions page (v24.21.0):

1. "This feature does not protect against malicious code." Permission model is seat-belt, not security boundary. SECURITY.md reiterates: permission model is not a security boundary against intentional misuse/compromised process; Node.js trusts code it is asked to run.

2. Wildcard behavior: "After passing a wildcard character (*) all subsequent characters will be ignored. For example: /home/*.js will work similar to /home/*." So `--allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js` is equivalent to `/srv/jobs/*` — it grants read to everything in that directory tree (wildcard added if dir exists). Also "automatically add a wildcard (*) if the specified directory exists" — /srv/jobs/*.js — hmm, the wildcard is after *.js... The specified directory pattern /srv/jobs/*.js — wildcard char appears, everything after ignored, so it's /srv/jobs/* ... Actually stated: "/home/*.js will work similar to /home/*." So the grant broadens to all files in /srv/jobs.

3. Symbolic links: "Symbolic links will be followed even to locations outside of the set of paths that access has been granted to. Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files and directories." — must ensure no granted paths contain relative symlinks. So the premise "job directories may contain relative symbolic links" directly violates documented constraint. This is disqualifying.

4. --env-file: "certain flags such as --env-file ... are designed to read files before environment initialization. As a result, such flags are not subject to the rules of the Permission Model." So env-file can load an env file outside the read list — that's documented behavior; it bypasses the model. That means the read grant is not actually a complete inventory of what's read. For tenant isolation, that means the env file read is unrestricted; need to treat env file as trusted operator input, or note it's not subject to permission model.

5. File descriptors: "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model." So passing an already-open fd bypasses restrictions — mechanism useful only for trusted code; cannot be used with untrusted job code.

6. Workers: The permissions page says "The model does not inherit to a worker thread." But SECURITY.md says "Workers inherit the permission restrictions of their parent process. Passing an empty or modified execArgv to a worker does not grant it additional permissions." That's a direct conflict between the two version-matched sources. The user explicitly asks: "If the sources do not establish one consistent worker-inheritance answer, state the limitation rather than silently choosing a convenient claim." So we must flag this conflict: permissions.html#permission-model-constraints says "The model does not inherit to a worker thread", while SECURITY.md's "Permission Model Boundaries" section says workers inherit the parent's restrictions. No consistent documented answer; mark UNVERIFIED for production behavior; next evidence target: worker_threads docs for v24.21.0 or permission-model tests in the repo.

7. --allow-worker with untrusted code: workers allow spawning worker_threads; combined with child_process? Not granted. But --allow-worker + execArgv? If workers can be spawned with arbitrary Linux... Actually worker_threads with permission model: if allow-worker granted, code can create workers; whether restrictions persist is the conflicting question. Also arbitrary code could pass execArgv.

8. --permission-audit in staging: audit mode does not deny; useful only to discover required permissions, not isolation. Fine as deployment discovery, but it's not a boundary even in staging if staging handles customer data.

9. Also: --allow-child-process not granted, native addons restricted, WASI restricted, inspector restricted. But: "OpenSSL engines cannot be requested at runtime"; "Run-Time Loadable Extensions cannot be loaded when the Permission Model is enabled, affecting the sqlite module." But node:sqlite file system access not guaranteed — "It does not guarantee that users will not be able to access the file system through other means, such as through the node:sqlite module." And SECURITY.md: node:sqlite DatabaseSync operates with same file-system privileges; SQL pragmas (ATTACH) not intercepted. So even under --permission, customer JS could open sqlite and read files via ATTACH DATABASE. Wait — the permissions page says the model restricts fs through node:fs, and "does not guarantee that users will not be able to access the file system through other means, such as through the node:sqlite module." So tenant isolation unattainable with node:sqlite available. Also process._debugProcess() bypass: any sandboxed process with no grants can force another Node process on same host/user to open inspector. So must run tenants under different OS users / OS-level isolation.

10. Also node API: process._debugProcess; also v8.setFlagsFromString can set V8 flags not subject to permission model.

11. Entrypoints: by default entrypoints included in allowed read list — main script; fine.

Decision: Cannot certify; permission model cannot be sole tenant-isolation boundary for untrusted customer JS. Need OS-level isolation (containers, separate OS users per tenant), reject symlink premise, remove fd passing and env-file reliance as bypasses, drop --allow-worker for untrusted code, keep audit mode for trusted app code discovery, use drop() post-init maybe. The docs explicitly state "does not protect against malicious code" — so sole boundary is contradicting docs.

Also worker-inheritance conflict: must state both. The two sources conflict. Also note permissions page "The model does not inherit to a worker thread" could be dated? But we only have these two docs; state conflict and recommend verifying with worker_threads docs (https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/worker_threads.html) as next evidence target.
